issues.legal_issue: Partition of a joint estate held by limited female co-heirs for separate enjoyment does not itself authorize one co-heir to alienate the estate’s corpus, although consent may be inferred from the circumstances.
material_facts: Three limited female co-heirs divided the property and took separate possession of their respective shares.
One co-heir made transfers from property in her separate possession without obtaining express consent from the others.
The other co-heirs did not challenge the transfers, and the reversioners waited until after the death of the last limited owner to challenge them.
issues.conclusion: Separate possession following partition did not by itself authorize an alienation of the corpus, but the circumstances justified presuming the other co-heirs’ consent; the transfer was not invalid on the ground that express consent had not been obtained.
issues.legal_principle: The estate of co-heirs holding as limited owners remains a joint estate; partition for separate enjoyment of income does not prejudice survivorship or a future reversioner, and an alienation by one co-heir ordinarily cannot bind the estate without the others’ authority. Such a transfer is voidable at the instance of the other limited owners or the reversioners, and consent may be inferred from the circumstances. The Court applied the principles in Appalasuri v. Kannamma, approved in Gauri Nath Kakaji v. Mt. Gaya Kuer.

predicates.limited_heirs_alienation_dispute: The proceeding concerns an alienation from an estate held by multiple female heirs as limited owners.
predicates.joint_estate_partitioned_for_separate_en: The co-heirs divided possession of the estate for separate enjoyment without creating separate absolute estates.
predicates.transfer_from_separately_possessed_prope: One co-heir transferred property that was in her separate possession.
predicates.coheirs_never_challenged_transfers: The other co-heirs did not challenge the transfers during their lifetimes.
predicates.reversioners_delayed_challenge_until_aft: The reversioners waited until after the last limited owner died to challenge the transfers.

issues.definition: When co-heirs hold a joint limited estate, separate possession alone does not authorize one heir to alienate its corpus, but the other heirs’ consent may be presumed if they did not challenge the transfers and the reversioners delayed their challenge until after the last limited owner died.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee may receive protection under the rule against denying a transferor’s later-acquired title when the limited owner who made the transfer later becomes the sole surviving holder of the estate.
material_facts: A limited owner made transfers while her two co-heirs were alive.
After those co-heirs died, she came into exclusive possession of the entire estate.
The transferees and their successors claimed protection for the transfers after the transferor’s later-acquired position in the estate.
issues.conclusion: The transferees were entitled to protection under section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act, consistent with the equitable principle of feeding the grant by estoppel.
issues.legal_principle: Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act embodies the equitable principle of feeding the grant by estoppel. The Court held that the transferees could claim its protection when the transferor later came into exclusive possession of the estate; it also observed that this issue lost importance once consent of the other co-heirs was presumed.

predicates.limited_owner_transfer_dispute: The proceeding concerns a transfer made by a person holding property as a limited owner.
predicates.transferor_later_became_sole_holder_of_e: The transferor later became the sole surviving holder in possession of the estate.
predicates.transferees_claim_protection_for_transfe: The transferees or their successors sought protection for the transfer based on the transferor’s later position in the estate.

issues.definition: A transferee claiming protection for a limited owner’s transfer is entitled to that protection when the transferor later becomes the sole surviving holder of the estate.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant’s acceptance of the compensation fixed for improvements may itself constitute an election under section 51, making a further opportunity to elect unnecessary.
material_facts: The transferees had made valuable constructions on the land, including educational and residential facilities.
The claimants accepted the compensation amount determined by the trial court.
The record indicated that the claimants were neither able nor inclined to pay for the improvements.
issues.conclusion: Acceptance of the amount fixed by the trial court constituted the claimants’ election under section 51, and the High Court was not justified in remanding the case to provide a fresh opportunity to elect.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act, the election concerning compensation for improvements may be established by the claimant’s conduct. In the circumstances, accepting the compensation fixed by the trial court itself amounted to making the choice, so a further opportunity to elect was unnecessary.

predicates.section_51_improvements_dispute: The proceeding concerns the choice available to a claimant in a dispute involving improvements made on property.
predicates.valuable_improvements_made_on_property: The transferees made valuable constructions or other substantial improvements on the property.
predicates.claimants_accepted_trial_court_compensat: The claimants accepted the compensation amount determined by the trial court.
predicates.claimants_unable_or_uninclined_to_pay_fo: The claimants were neither able nor inclined to pay for the improvements.

issues.definition: When claimants accept the trial court’s compensation for valuable improvements and are unable or uninclined to pay for those improvements, their acceptance constitutes their election and no fresh opportunity to elect is required.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court will not interfere with a High Court’s factual finding based on its assessment of the evidence concerning whether an alienation was made for legal necessity.
material_facts: The High Court assessed the evidence and found that two transfers were not made for legal and pressing necessity.
The appellants challenged that finding in the appeal to the Supreme Court.
The challenge depended on the weight and sufficiency of the evidence considered by the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court would not interfere with the High Court’s finding concerning the absence of legal necessity.
issues.legal_principle: The quantum of evidence sufficient to satisfy a court on a factual issue is within that court’s discretion; the Supreme Court therefore would not disturb the High Court’s finding on the evidence in this case.

predicates.civil_appeal_from_high_court: The proceeding is a civil appeal from a High Court judgment.
predicates.high_court_finding_based_on_evidence_ass: The High Court made the challenged finding after assessing the evidence.
predicates.challenge_depends_on_weight_of_evidence: The challenge asks the appellate court to reassess the weight or sufficiency of the evidence.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal, a factual finding reached by the High Court through assessment of evidence is not disturbed when the challenge depends on reweighing that evidence.
